document.title: Afghanistan: The Taliban's Decision-Making Process and Leadership Structure (Islama 09531)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban Biography: The Structure and Leadership of the Taliban 1996-2002
document.note: [Confidential] Updates the 1997 review: Omar is stronger than ever and enforces policy via the Ministry to Propagate Virtue and Prevent Vice. The Inner and Outer shuras are weakening while the Ulema Shura gains influence. Omar, perhaps under bin Ladin's influence, may be more sympathetic to pan-Islamism. Taliban decision-making remains opaque. Excised.

events.description: Formation of the Taliban movement.
US missile strike hit Haqqani's area in Khost.
US Embassy Islamabad cable on Taliban leadership.
Taliban offensive in the north, with Berudah and Dadullah involved.
Governor of Ghazni Mullah Yar Mohammad killed.
Razzaq captured by northern forces in Mazar-i-Sharif, released months later.
Razzaq led disastrous Taliban advance north after fall of Kabul.
Taliban captured Kabul; Kabul Shura formed.
Mass meeting of mullahs in Kandahar named Omar 'Amir'.
Ulema convocation in Kabul justified Taliban relations with bin Ladin.
Taliban capture of Kabul; the Kabul Shura (Caretaker Council) formed afterwards.
Mass meeting of mullahs in Kandahar named Omar 'Amir', apparently organized by the Ulema Shura.
Ulema convocation in Kabul justified the Taliban's relations with bin Ladin.
U.S. missile strikes hit Haqqani's area in Khost.
Taliban assault on the north; Berudah was key military strategist, Dadullah involved.
Razzaq captured by Northern forces in Mazar-i-Sharif; released months later.
Razzaq led disastrous Taliban advance north after the fall of Kabul.
Mullah Borjan was killed shortly before Kabul fell.
Ghazni governor Mullah Yar Mohammad killed, reportedly by Shi'as.
Omar quoted at least twice criticizing the U.S. presence in the Gulf.
Zakari served as political commissar in the Kunduz area for much of 1998.
U.S. Embassy Islamabad cable on the Taliban's decision-making and leadership structure.
Formation of the Taliban movement in late 1994.
Fall of the communist regime in Afghanistan; corrupt mujahideen commanders then ruled the Kandahar area.
U.S. Embassy produced its December 1997 benchmark review of 'who's who in the Taliban', updated by this message.
U.S. Embassy Islamabad cable on the Taliban's decision-making process and leadership structure sent to State Department.

sources_cited: 97 Islamabad 11233 (Dec 1997 benchmark review of Taliban who's who)
key_claims: Mullah Omar is the preeminent Taliban decision-maker; influence is judged by closeness to him.
Omar is the major proponent of letting bin Ladin stay as a guest and may be influenced toward pan-Islamist thinking.
Omar enforces control via the vice ministry (Wali) and intelligence ministry (Hamdullah) and rotates officials.
Rabbani, Hassan and Haqqani hold independent power bases but are probably not serious rivals.
Haqqani commands loyalty of Khost-based Zadran tribesmen and is close to Arab and Pakistani Islamists.
Haji Bashir is a Maiwand-born businessman reported as drug trade player and financier of the Taliban.
Jalil serves as conduit to Arab militants, and Zakari justifies the Taliban-bin Ladin relationship.
The inner and outer shuras are weakening while the Ulema Shura has gained influence.
Haqqani should be considered a Taliban figure with his own Zadran power base and is a 'Khost-Paktia-Paktika' pretender to the Taliban throne.
Haqqani is close to Arab and Pakistani Islamists; the August 1998 US missile strike hit his area in Khost.
Taliban formal institutions (Inner, Outer, Kabul and Ulema Shuras) lack real authority under Omar's autocratic style.
The Ulema Shura organized the convocation that justified Taliban relations with bin Ladin in Kabul in September 1998.
No ordered succession exists; Rabbani is the conventional successor but Kandahar governor Mullah Hassan is a possibility.
Arab and Pakistani extremists in Afghanistan could play a role in a succession struggle.
